title: Novel Writing
subtitle: Build a character, choose a narrator, and open a novel that keeps its promise

lessons.title: Construire un personnage
lessons.description: The craftsman's toolkit for building a fictional character: the telling physical detail, the psychology of desire and contradiction, and the difference between a round character and a flat one.

blocks.heading: Le portrait physique et la première impression
blocks.body: Classic character portraiture does not inventory every feature; it selects one or two telling details that carry symbolic weight and make the character memorable. A trembling hand, a way of avoiding eye contact, a coat worn too long — these details work harder than a full catalogue of hair colour, height, and clothing ever could.

examples.french: Elle portait ses cheveux gris comme un défi, sans jamais les teindre.
examples.english: She wore her grey hair like a challenge, never dyeing it.

examples.french: Un seul détail suffit parfois : ses mains tremblaient légèrement quand elle mentait.
examples.english: One detail is sometimes enough: her hands trembled slightly when she lied.

examples.french: Le romancier évite l'inventaire : il choisit le trait qui en dit long.
examples.english: The novelist avoids the inventory: he chooses the trait that speaks volumes.

examples.french: Son regard fuyant trahissait une gêne qu'aucune phrase n'aurait pu nommer.
examples.english: His evasive gaze betrayed an unease no sentence could have named.

examples.french: La première impression se construit en une phrase, ou elle ne se construit pas.
examples.english: The first impression is built in one sentence, or it isn't built at all.

blocks.tip: Choose one physical detail that will pay off later in the plot — a scar the character keeps touching, a limp that slows a chase scene.

blocks.heading: La psychologie : motivation, désir, contradiction
blocks.body: A believable character needs a precise driving desire — a want — set against an internal contradiction: something feared or needed that pulls against that want. This tension, more than any biography, is what creates dramatic interest and keeps a character from collapsing into a single trait.

examples.french: Chaque personnage a besoin d'un désir précis, même s'il l'ignore lui-même.
examples.english: Every character needs a precise desire, even if they are unaware of it.

examples.french: La contradiction rend un personnage vivant : il veut partir, mais il reste.
examples.english: Contradiction makes a character alive: he wants to leave, but he stays.

examples.french: Le conflit intérieur oppose ce que le personnage désire à ce qu'il redoute.
examples.english: Inner conflict pits what the character desires against what he dreads.

examples.french: Sans motivation claire, même les actions les plus spectaculaires paraissent gratuites.
examples.english: Without clear motivation, even the most spectacular actions seem gratuitous.

examples.french: L'ambivalence n'est pas une faiblesse d'écriture : c'est souvent son but.
examples.english: Ambivalence is not a writing flaw: it is often the goal.

blocks.tip: Ask what the character wants on the surface, and what they actually need underneath — the gap between the two often drives the whole plot.

blocks.heading: Personnage rond, personnage plat : la vraisemblance
blocks.body: Not every character needs equal depth: a round character keeps the capacity to surprise across the whole novel, while a flat character serves a single function and asks for none. The danger lies in confusing a flat character with a lazy one — the cliché sets in exactly when a single trait is left to stand in for a whole person.

examples.french: Le personnage rond garde la capacité de nous surprendre jusqu'à la dernière page.
examples.english: The round character keeps the ability to surprise us until the very last page.

examples.french: Le personnage plat reste utile : il ne demande pas de développement, seulement de la fonction.
examples.english: The flat character remains useful: he requires no development, only a function.

examples.french: Le cliché s'installe dès que le trait remplace la personne tout entière.
examples.english: The cliché sets in as soon as the trait replaces the whole person.

examples.french: La vraisemblance ne copie pas le réel : elle construit une cohérence interne.
examples.english: Verisimilitude does not copy reality: it builds an internal coherence.

examples.french: Un personnage secondaire trop caricatural peut fragiliser tout le roman.
examples.english: An overly caricatured secondary character can weaken the whole novel.

blocks.tip: If you can predict everything a character will do in every scene, they are still flat — give them at least one contradictory choice.

items.example: Le personnage principal n'apparaît qu'au deuxième chapitre.
items.exampleEnglish: The main character does not appear until the second chapter.

items.example: Le protagoniste refuse tout au long du roman le rôle qu'on lui assigne.
items.exampleEnglish: The protagonist refuses, throughout the novel, the role he is assigned.

items.example: L'antagoniste n'apparaît jamais en personne, seulement dans les lettres qu'il envoie.
items.exampleEnglish: The antagonist never appears in person, only in the letters he sends.

items.example: Le portrait tient en trois phrases, pas en trois pages.
items.exampleEnglish: The portrait fits in three sentences, not three pages.

items.example: La caractérisation se fait autant par les actes que par la description.
items.exampleEnglish: Characterisation happens as much through actions as through description.

items.example: Un seul trait de caractère, bien choisi, vaut mieux qu'une liste entière.
items.exampleEnglish: One well-chosen character trait is worth more than a whole list.

items.example: La psychologie du personnage se révèle par petites touches, jamais d'un coup.
items.exampleEnglish: The character's psychology is revealed in small touches, never all at once.

items.example: Le physique du personnage compte moins que la façon dont il l'habite.
items.exampleEnglish: The character's physical appearance matters less than how he inhabits it.

items.example: L'apparence soignée cache une vie parfaitement désordonnée.
items.exampleEnglish: The tidy appearance hides a perfectly disordered life.

items.example: Sa personnalité se dessine surtout dans ses silences.
items.exampleEnglish: Her personality is drawn mostly in her silences.

items.example: Un défaut bien choisi humanise un personnage plus vite qu'une qualité.
items.exampleEnglish: A well-chosen flaw humanises a character faster than a virtue does.

items.example: Ses qualités mêmes finissent par se retourner contre elle.
items.exampleEnglish: Her very virtues eventually turn against her.

items.example: Sans motivation claire, l'action du personnage sonne faux.
items.exampleEnglish: Without clear motivation, the character's action rings false.

items.example: Le désir du personnage doit être visible dès la première scène.
items.exampleEnglish: The character's desire must be visible from the first scene.

items.example: Le conflit intérieur du personnage vaut souvent plus que le conflit extérieur.
items.exampleEnglish: A character's inner conflict is often worth more than the outer one.

items.example: Une contradiction assumée rend le personnage plus crédible qu'une cohérence parfaite.
items.exampleEnglish: An owned contradiction makes a character more believable than perfect consistency.

items.example: L'ambivalence du personnage se lit dans ce qu'il ne dit jamais franchement.
items.exampleEnglish: The character's ambivalence shows in what he never says outright.

items.example: L'histoire personnelle du personnage n'a pas besoin d'être racontée en entier.
items.exampleEnglish: A character's backstory does not need to be told in full.

items.example: L'évolution du personnage se joue en trois moments, pas davantage.
items.exampleEnglish: The character's arc plays out in three moments, no more.

items.example: Un personnage secondaire réussi reste en mémoire après une seule scène.
items.exampleEnglish: A successful secondary character stays in memory after just one scene.

items.english: the extra, the minor background character
items.example: Même un figurant mérite une phrase qui lui donne une existence propre.
items.exampleEnglish: Even a background character deserves one sentence that gives him his own existence.

items.example: Le personnage rond garde toujours une capacité de surprise.
items.exampleEnglish: The round character always keeps a capacity to surprise.

items.example: Le personnage plat sert une seule fonction, sans jamais se développer.
items.exampleEnglish: The flat character serves a single function, without ever developing.

items.example: C'est la nuance qui sauve un personnage du cliché.
items.exampleEnglish: It is nuance that saves a character from cliché.

items.example: La complexité d'un personnage ne se mesure pas au nombre de ses défauts.
items.exampleEnglish: A character's complexity is not measured by the number of his flaws.

items.example: Le premier cliché qui vient à l'esprit est presque toujours à éviter.
items.exampleEnglish: The first cliché that comes to mind is almost always the one to avoid.

items.example: Le stéréotype rassure le lecteur en lui épargnant toute surprise.
items.exampleEnglish: The stereotype reassures the reader by sparing them any surprise.

items.example: La caricature exagère un trait au point d'effacer tout le reste.
items.exampleEnglish: The caricature exaggerates one trait to the point of erasing everything else.

items.english: to embody, to give flesh to
items.example: Le romancier incarne son idée dans un personnage, jamais dans un discours.
items.exampleEnglish: The novelist embodies his idea in a character, never in a speech.

items.example: Le roman dépeint un homme incapable de nommer ce qu'il ressent.
items.exampleEnglish: The novel depicts a man unable to name what he feels.

items.example: L'auteur esquisse le personnage en une phrase, puis le laisse agir.
items.exampleEnglish: The author sketches the character in one sentence, then lets him act.

items.example: Trois répliques suffisent à camper un personnage secondaire.
items.exampleEnglish: Three lines are enough to vividly establish a secondary character.

items.example: Un personnage crédible n'est pas un personnage sympathique.
items.exampleEnglish: A believable character is not the same as a likeable one.

items.example: Il reste attachant précisément parce qu'il échoue si souvent.
items.exampleEnglish: He remains endearing precisely because he fails so often.

items.example: Son sourire final reste volontairement ambigu.
items.exampleEnglish: His final smile remains deliberately ambiguous.

items.example: Un portrait nuancé résiste à la fois à l'admiration et au rejet.
items.exampleEnglish: A nuanced portrait resists both admiration and rejection.

items.example: La cohérence d'un personnage ne dépend pas de sa ressemblance au réel.
items.exampleEnglish: A character's coherence does not depend on resembling reality.

items.example: La vraisemblance d'un personnage tient à sa cohérence, non à sa banalité.
items.exampleEnglish: A character's plausibility rests on his coherence, not on his ordinariness.

blocks.heading: L'imparfait de description et le passé simple d'action
blocks.body: In literary narration, the imparfait paints backgrounds, habitual states, and ongoing character traits — a kind of freeze-frame — while the passé simple marks the punctual, completed action that moves the plot forward. The alternation itself is a signal: it tells the reader exactly when a portrait pauses and the story resumes.

examples.french: Elle avait les yeux clairs et ne souriait presque jamais. Ce matin-là, pourtant, elle sourit.
examples.english: She had light eyes and almost never smiled. That morning, however, she smiled.
examples.note: imparfait for the standing trait, passé simple for the break

examples.french: Il portait toujours ce manteau trop grand. Il l'enleva, pour la première fois, devant elle.
examples.english: He always wore that coat too big for him. He took it off, for the first time, in front of her.

examples.french: La ville dormait encore quand il sortit sans un bruit.
examples.english: The city was still asleep when he went out without a sound.

examples.french: Elle détestait le silence ; ce jour-là, elle le choisit.
examples.english: She hated silence; that day, she chose it.

examples.french: Le passé simple interrompt l'imparfait comme un coup frappé dans le calme.
examples.english: The passé simple interrupts the imperfect like a knock struck in the calm.

blocks.tip: Read a paragraph aloud: if it stays in the imparfait, you are still painting the portrait; the passé simple verb is where the story actually starts moving.

blocks.heading: Les relatives pour caractériser : dont, ce qui, ce que
blocks.body: At this level, character description leans on compact relative constructions: 'dont' replaces a clunky 'de qui / de quoi / duquel', while 'ce qui' and 'ce que' let a writer characterise a person through an indefinite, unnamed antecedent — what struck people, what she hid — rather than a flat list of named traits.

examples.french: C'était un homme dont on ne savait jamais s'il plaisantait.
examples.english: He was a man you could never tell was joking or not.

examples.french: Ce qui frappait chez elle, ce n'était pas la beauté, mais l'aplomb.
examples.english: What struck people about her was not her beauty, but her self-assurance.

examples.french: Elle cachait ce qu'elle pensait derrière une politesse parfaite.
examples.english: She hid what she was thinking behind a perfect politeness.

examples.french: Le personnage dont je parle n'apparaît que dans les trois derniers chapitres.
examples.english: The character I am speaking of only appears in the last three chapters.

examples.french: Tout ce qu'on savait de lui tenait dans une seule phrase, jamais complétée.
examples.english: Everything known about him fit into a single sentence, never completed.

blocks.tip: Reach for 'dont' whenever the relative clause would otherwise need an awkward 'de + pronoun' construction.

passages.title: Portrait d'une inconnue
passages.french: Elle s'appelait Odile, mais personne au village ne l'appelait ainsi depuis la mort de son mari. On disait « la veuve », comme si le mot suffisait à la décrire tout entière. Elle portait ses cheveux gris comme un défi, sans jamais les teindre, et ne souriait presque jamais — sauf, disait-on, le mardi, jour du marché, où elle vendait ses légumes en plaisantant avec les enfants. Ce détail dérangeait tout le monde : une femme si dure ne devrait pas savoir rire ainsi. Elle détestait le silence de sa maison vide ; pourtant, chaque soir, elle éteignait la radio dès la première note de musique. Personne ne comprenait pourquoi. Peut-être qu'elle ne le comprenait pas non plus.
passages.english: Her name was Odile, but no one in the village had called her that since her husband's death. They said "the widow," as though the word were enough to describe her entirely. She wore her grey hair like a challenge, never dyeing it, and almost never smiled — except, they said, on Tuesdays, market day, when she sold her vegetables while joking with the children. That detail unsettled everyone: a woman so hard should not know how to laugh like that. She hated the silence of her empty house; and yet, every evening, she switched off the radio at the very first note of music. No one understood why. Perhaps she did not understand it herself.

questions.prompt: What detail unsettles the villagers about Odile?
options: That she laughs and jokes on market day
That she never leaves her house
That she refuses to sell her vegetables
That she moved away after her husband's death
questions.answer: That she laughs and jokes on market day

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the final sentence, 'Peut-être qu'elle ne le comprenait pas non plus'?
options: It leaves the character's contradiction genuinely unresolved
It explains exactly why she turns off the radio
It reveals that Odile is lying to the village
It confirms the villagers' nickname for her is accurate
questions.answer: It leaves the character's contradiction genuinely unresolved

lessons.title: Le narrateur
lessons.description: Choosing a narrative voice: first versus third person, the three focalisations, and how far a novelist can trust — or deliberately not trust — the narrator to tell the truth.

blocks.heading: Première personne, troisième personne : effets de la voix
blocks.body: First person narration locks the reader inside one consciousness, trading reliability for intimacy; third person can range from a close, almost first-person closeness to a distant, panoramic sweep. Neither choice is neutral: it decides what the reader is allowed to know, and when.

examples.french: À la première personne, le lecteur ne sait jamais plus que le narrateur lui-même.
examples.english: In the first person, the reader never knows more than the narrator himself.

examples.french: La troisième personne peut se tenir tout près d'un personnage, ou très loin de tous.
examples.english: The third person can stand very close to one character, or very far from all of them.

examples.french: Changer de personne en cours de roman est un risque, mais parfois un risque payant.
examples.english: Switching person partway through a novel is a risk, but sometimes a rewarding one.

examples.french: La deuxième personne reste rare : elle accuse le lecteur autant qu'elle le désigne.
examples.english: The second person remains rare: it accuses the reader as much as it designates him.

examples.french: Le choix de la voix précède presque toujours le choix de l'intrigue elle-même.
examples.english: The choice of voice almost always comes before the choice of plot itself.

blocks.tip: Draft the opening page in both first and third person before committing — the plot often reveals what it actually needs.

blocks.heading: La focalisation : interne, externe, zéro
blocks.body: Focalisation interne restricts the narration to one character's knowledge and perception; focalisation externe reports only what an outside observer could see, withholding all interior thought; focalisation zéro is the traditional omniscient stance, moving freely between minds and across time. A novel can mix all three, but a shift must always be a deliberate choice, not a slip.

examples.french: La focalisation interne enferme le lecteur dans une seule conscience à la fois.
examples.english: Internal focalisation locks the reader inside a single consciousness at a time.

examples.french: La focalisation externe se contente de décrire les gestes, jamais les pensées.
examples.english: External focalisation is content to describe gestures, never thoughts.

examples.french: La focalisation zéro permet au narrateur de savoir ce qu'aucun personnage ne sait.
examples.english: Zero focalisation lets the narrator know what no single character knows.

examples.french: Un narrateur omniscient qui entre dans toutes les consciences risque de les aplatir.
examples.english: An omniscient narrator who enters every consciousness risks flattening them all.

examples.french: Changer de focalisation d'un chapitre à l'autre reste plus sûr qu'à l'intérieur d'une même scène.
examples.english: Shifting focalisation from one chapter to the next is safer than doing so within a single scene.

blocks.tip: If you must shift focalisation mid-scene, mark it with a clear signal — a paragraph break, a change of tense — so the reader never feels cheated.

blocks.heading: Le narrateur fiable ou non : jusqu'où faire confiance ?
blocks.body: An unreliable narrator does not simply lie: they may misunderstand their own story, minimise what shames them, or filter events through a bias the reader must learn to detect. The technique works only if the text leaves the reader enough evidence — contradictions, omissions, tone — to reconstruct the truth the narrator will not, or cannot, state directly.

examples.french: Le narrateur non fiable ne ment pas toujours : il se trompe parfois lui-même.
examples.english: The unreliable narrator does not always lie: he sometimes deceives himself.

examples.french: La fiabilité du narrateur se juge aux détails qu'il choisit de taire.
examples.english: A narrator's reliability is judged by the details he chooses to leave unsaid.

examples.french: Un narrateur intrusif commente l'histoire au lieu de se contenter de la raconter.
examples.english: An intrusive narrator comments on the story instead of simply telling it.

examples.french: Le lecteur implicite doit toujours pouvoir reconstruire ce que le narrateur cache.
examples.english: The implied reader must always be able to reconstruct what the narrator hides.

examples.french: La subjectivité assumée d'un narrateur vaut mieux qu'une fausse objectivité.
examples.english: A narrator's acknowledged subjectivity is worth more than a false objectivity.

blocks.tip: Leave at least one small, verifiable contradiction in an unreliable narrator's account — it is the reader's only anchor to the real story.

items.english: extradiegetic (narrating from outside the story world)
items.example: Un narrateur extradiégétique s'adresse au lecteur depuis l'extérieur du récit.

items.example: La fiabilité du narrateur se juge aux détails qu'il choisit de taire.

items.example: Le chapitre entier n'est qu'un long monologue intérieur.

items.example: Le style indirect libre fond la voix du narrateur dans celle du personnage.

items.example: Le discours indirect résume les propos sans prétendre à l'exactitude mot à mot.

blocks.heading: Le discours indirect libre : ni citation, ni résumé
blocks.body: Free indirect discourse reports a character's thought or speech without a reporting verb ('il pensa que') and without quotation marks — it keeps the character's own vocabulary and exclamations, but shifts pronouns and tenses as reported speech normally does. The result blends the narrator's voice with the character's own, letting the text hold both perspectives in a single unmarked sentence.

examples.french: Elle regarda l'horloge. Encore en retard, comme toujours.
examples.english: She looked at the clock. Late again, as always.
examples.note: no reporting verb: the second sentence is her unspoken thought

examples.french: Il sortit dans la rue. Quel froid, tout de même, pour un mois de mai !
examples.english: He went out into the street. What cold, all the same, for the month of May!
examples.note: exclamation kept intact, no quotation marks

examples.french: Elle se demanda pourquoi il n'était pas encore arrivé.
examples.english: She wondered why he had not yet arrived.
examples.note: compare: this is ordinary indirect discourse, with a reporting verb

examples.french: Pourquoi n'était-il pas encore arrivé ? Elle ne comprenait plus rien.
examples.english: Why had he not yet arrived? She no longer understood anything.
examples.note: same content, now in style indirect libre

examples.french: Le style indirect libre n'appartient ni tout à fait au narrateur, ni tout à fait au personnage.
examples.english: Free indirect discourse belongs neither entirely to the narrator nor entirely to the character.

blocks.tip: Test a suspected passage of style indirect libre by removing the surrounding narration — if it still reads as a natural thought or outburst, the style indirect libre is at work.

blocks.heading: Les décalages temporels de l'analepse et de la prolepse
blocks.body: A flashback (analepse) or flash-forward (prolepse) usually requires a tense shift to signal the jump: the plus-que-parfait marks an analepse from a passé simple or imparfait main narrative, while the futur or conditionnel can mark a prolepse. The shift itself is what tells the reader which timeline they are now in, without needing an explicit 'des années plus tard'.

examples.french: Il se souvint, ce soir-là, du jour où son père était parti sans un mot.
examples.english: That evening, he remembered the day his father had left without a word.

examples.french: Elle ignorait encore qu'elle ne reverrait jamais cette maison.
examples.english: She did not yet know that she would never see that house again.
examples.note: conditionnel signals a prolepse from within the imparfait

examples.french: Vingt ans plus tard, il comprendrait enfin ce que ce silence avait voulu dire.
examples.english: Twenty years later, he would finally understand what that silence had meant.
examples.note: futur du passé (conditionnel) marks the flash-forward

examples.french: Le plus-que-parfait renvoie toujours à un passé antérieur au passé du récit.
examples.english: The plus-que-parfait always points to a past earlier than the story's own past.

examples.french: Sans marqueur temporel clair, l'analepse et la prolepse désorientent plus qu'elles n'éclairent.
examples.english: Without a clear temporal marker, the flashback and the flash-forward disorient more than they illuminate.

blocks.tip: Anchor every analepse or prolepse with at least one clear tense shift — a stray plus-que-parfait is often the only signal the reader gets.

passages.title: Le carnet de Julien
passages.french: Je note ceci pour moi seul, et je jure que je dirai la vérité, même si personne d'autre ne la lira jamais. Le soir où tout a changé, je n'ai rien fait de mal. Enfin — presque rien. J'étais rentré tard, c'est vrai, et je n'avais pas répondu à ses appels. Mais je n'avais pas vu l'heure, voilà tout ; le temps m'avait échappé, comme il m'échappe toujours quand je travaille. Elle m'a accusé de l'avoir oubliée exprès. C'est faux, évidemment. Je n'oublie jamais rien exprès. Enfin, je crois.
passages.english: I am writing this for myself alone, and I swear I will tell the truth, even if no one else ever reads it. On the evening everything changed, I did nothing wrong. Well — almost nothing. I had come home late, that much is true, and I had not answered her calls. But I simply had not noticed the time; time always gets away from me when I am working. She accused me of forgetting her on purpose. That is false, obviously. I never forget anything on purpose. Well, I think.

lessons.title: L'incipit
lessons.description: The novel's opening as a contract with the reader: the weight of the first sentence, the choice between in medias res and setting the scene, and how to hook without cheating the promise that follows.

blocks.heading: La première phrase : un contrat de lecture
blocks.body: The incipit is not decoration: it is a contract. The first sentence sets expectations for tone, register, and pace that the rest of the novel is bound to honour, or to break only on purpose. A reader forgives almost anything except a first sentence that lied about what kind of book was starting.

examples.french: La première phrase promet un ton que tout le roman devra tenir, ou trahir volontairement.
examples.english: The first sentence promises a tone the whole novel must honour, or deliberately betray.

examples.french: Le lecteur pardonne une intrigue lente, rarement une promesse d'ouverture non tenue.
examples.english: The reader forgives a slow plot, rarely a broken opening promise.

examples.french: Un bon incipit installe le monde du roman en une seule phrase.
examples.english: A good incipit sets up the novel's world in a single sentence.

examples.french: La formule choc de la première ligne se paie souvent d'une baisse de rythme ensuite.
examples.english: The punchy formula of the first line often costs a drop in pace afterward.

examples.french: Le contrat de lecture se signe dès le premier paragraphe, sans retour possible.
examples.english: The reading contract is signed within the first paragraph, with no going back.

blocks.tip: Write the last page of your novel before the first — knowing the ending tells you exactly what promise the opening sentence needs to make.

blocks.heading: Entrer in medias res ou planter le décor
blocks.body: A novel can open in medias res, dropping the reader into an action already underway, or it can first plant le décor — establish setting, mood, and cadre spatio-temporel before any event occurs. Neither is superior; the choice depends on whether suspense or atmosphere is the novel's first priority.

examples.french: Entrer in medias res prive le lecteur d'explications, mais capte son attention aussitôt.
examples.english: Opening in medias res deprives the reader of explanations, but captures attention immediately.

examples.french: Planter le décor avant l'action installe une atmosphère que l'intrigue viendra ensuite troubler.
examples.english: Setting the scene before the action establishes an atmosphere the plot will later disturb.

examples.french: Le cadre spatio-temporel se fixe souvent en une ou deux phrases, jamais davantage.
examples.english: The spatio-temporal setting is usually fixed in one or two sentences, never more.

examples.french: Une exposition trop longue épuise la curiosité avant même que l'intrigue commence.
examples.english: An overly long exposition exhausts curiosity before the plot has even begun.

examples.french: Le seuil du texte — titre, épigraphe, dédicace — prépare déjà la lecture de l'incipit.
examples.english: The text's threshold — title, epigraph, dedication — already prepares the reading of the incipit.

blocks.tip: If your opening scene needs more than a paragraph of pure exposition before anything happens, consider starting later and folding the background in afterward.

blocks.heading: Créer l'accroche sans trahir la promesse
blocks.body: An accroche should intriguer or déconcerter just enough to make the reader keep going, but a hook is only honest if the novel actually delivers on what it suggested. A striking first line that promises a mystery the plot never resolves, or a comic tone the book abandons by chapter two, breaks the very contract it opened with.

examples.french: Une bonne accroche suscite la curiosité sans jamais révéler la totalité de l'enjeu.
examples.english: A good hook arouses curiosity without ever revealing the full stakes.

examples.french: Intriguer le lecteur ne suffit pas : il faut ensuite tenir la promesse posée dès l'incipit.
examples.english: Intriguing the reader is not enough: the promise set up in the incipit must then be kept.

examples.french: Un incipit saisissant peut aussi bien déconcerter que rassurer, selon le projet du roman.
examples.english: A striking incipit can either disconcert or reassure, depending on the novel's project.

examples.french: L'explicit répond souvent, des années plus tard dans le texte, à la promesse de l'incipit.
examples.english: The closing lines often answer, much later in the text, the promise made by the incipit.

examples.french: Capter l'attention en une phrase ne dispense jamais de la tenir sur trois cents pages.
examples.english: Capturing attention in one sentence never excuses failing to sustain it over three hundred pages.

blocks.tip: After drafting a striking opening line, check the whole manuscript against it — every hook it sets up must eventually pay off.

blocks.heading: Les temps de l'ouverture : présent de narration ou passé simple
blocks.body: Most classical incipits open in the passé simple, the tense of literary narration proper, but a growing number open in the présent de narration to collapse the distance between reader and event, giving the very first sentence an immediacy the passé simple cannot match. The choice made in the first sentence is rarely reversed later — it sets the temporal register for the whole book.

examples.french: Ce matin-là, il ouvrit les yeux avant l'aube, sans savoir pourquoi.
examples.english: That morning, he opened his eyes before dawn, without knowing why.

examples.french: Ce matin, il ouvre les yeux avant l'aube, sans savoir pourquoi.
examples.english: This morning, he opens his eyes before dawn, without knowing why.
examples.note: présent de narration: immediate, almost cinematic

examples.french: Le présent de narration resserre la distance entre le lecteur et l'événement raconté.
examples.english: The present of narration tightens the distance between the reader and the event told.

examples.french: Le passé simple installe d'emblée un narrateur qui domine son récit de haut.
examples.english: The passé simple establishes from the outset a narrator who oversees his story from above.

examples.french: Le choix du temps verbal, dans l'incipit, se maintient rarement à moitié.
examples.english: The choice of tense, in the incipit, is rarely maintained only halfway.

blocks.tip: Read your opening paragraph in both tenses before committing — the présent de narration usually asks for shorter, punchier sentences than the passé simple does.

blocks.heading: L'inversion et la mise en relief dans la phrase d'ouverture
blocks.body: An opening sentence often inverts the expected word order — placing a complement, an adverb, or an adjective before the subject — to throw weight onto the very first word the reader encounters. This mise en relief is a deliberate craft choice: the word that opens the book is rarely there by accident.

examples.french: Loin de la ville, une maison attendait, seule, depuis des années.
examples.english: Far from the city, a house had been waiting, alone, for years.

examples.french: Jamais on n'avait vu un hiver pareil dans ce village.
examples.english: Never had such a winter been seen in this village.

examples.french: Grande était la maison, et pourtant personne n'y vivait plus.
examples.english: Great was the house, and yet no one lived there anymore.

examples.french: C'est un mardi, à l'aube, que tout a commencé.
examples.english: It was on a Tuesday, at dawn, that everything began.
examples.note: c'est... que construction highlighting the time

examples.french: La mise en relief d'une phrase d'ouverture guide le regard du lecteur avant même le sens.
examples.english: The emphatic structure of an opening sentence guides the reader's eye before it guides meaning.

blocks.tip: Whatever word or phrase you front in the opening sentence, make sure it is the one idea you most want the reader to carry into chapter two.

passages.title: Incipit sans titre
passages.french: La maison n'avait pas de porte, seulement un trou dans le mur que tout le monde appelait, par habitude, l'entrée. C'est un mardi, à l'aube, que Camille y posa le pied pour la première fois depuis vingt ans. Elle n'avait rien prévu de dire. Elle n'avait même pas prévu de venir. Et pourtant, la voici, debout sur ce seuil sans porte, incapable de faire un pas de plus, ni d'en faire un en arrière.
passages.english: The house had no door, only a hole in the wall that everyone, out of habit, called the entrance. It was on a Tuesday, at dawn, that Camille set foot there for the first time in twenty years. She had planned nothing to say. She had not even planned to come. And yet, here she is, standing on this doorless threshold, unable to take one more step forward, or one step back.

questions.prompt: Which opening strategy does this incipit primarily use?
options: It plants a striking image (the doorless house) before the character even acts
It opens fully in medias res, mid-action, with no scene-setting at all
It opens with an epigraph borrowed from another author
It begins with a long, unbroken block of exposition about Camille's past
questions.answer: It plants a striking image (the doorless house) before the character even acts

questions.prompt: What tense does the final sentence shift into, and what effect does that produce?
options: The présent de narration, tightening the distance to the moment
The plus-que-parfait, pushing the scene further into the past
The futur simple, promising what will happen next
The imparfait, softening the scene into a habitual memory
questions.answer: The présent de narration, tightening the distance to the moment

questions.prompt: The passage tells the reader exactly why Camille left twenty years earlier.

items.prompt: Translate into French.
items.english: A good hook arouses curiosity without ever revealing the full stakes.
items.answer: Une bonne accroche suscite la curiosité sans jamais révéler la totalité de l'enjeu.
acceptedAnswers: une bonne accroche suscite la curiosite sans jamais reveler la totalite de l'enjeu
une bonne accroche suscite la curiosite sans jamais reveler la totalite de lenjeu

items.prompt: Rebuild this sentence about the incipit.
items.answer: Un bon incipit installe le monde du roman en une seule phrase
items.english: A good incipit sets up the novel's world in a single sentence.

items.prompt: Le contrat de ___ se signe dès le premier paragraphe, sans retour possible.
items.tip: The implicit pact between the writer and their reader.

items.prompt: Quel terme désigne les toutes premières lignes d'une œuvre ?
Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.english: establishing setting and mood before the action
the closing lines of a work
what the opening commits the novel to deliver

items.prompt: Intriguer le lecteur ne suffit pas : il faut ensuite ___ la promesse posée dès l'incipit.
Une exposition narrative trop longue épuise généralement la curiosité du lecteur.
Translate: The reader forgives a slow plot, rarely a broken opening promise.
items.english: The reader forgives a slow plot, rarely a broken opening promise.
items.answer: Le lecteur pardonne une intrigue lente, rarement une promesse d'ouverture non tenue.
acceptedAnswers: le lecteur pardonne une intrigue lente, rarement une promesse d'ouverture non tenue
le lecteur pardonne une intrigue lente rarement une promesse douverture non tenue

items.prompt: Quel temps donne à la phrase d'ouverture une immédiateté presque cinématographique ?
Que promet essentiellement la première phrase d'un roman ?
options: Un contrat de lecture que le roman devra honorer
Le nombre total de chapitres du livre
Le nom complet de tous les personnages
La date exacte de publication du roman
items.answer: Un contrat de lecture que le roman devra honorer

items.prompt: Le ___ du texte — titre, épigraphe, dédicace — prépare déjà la lecture de l'incipit.
What is the risk of an opening that promises a mystery or comic tone the novel never delivers?
options: It breaks the reading contract set up by the incipit
It automatically makes the prose more literary
It has no effect, since only the ending matters
items.answer: It breaks the reading contract set up by the incipit

items.prompt: Entrer in medias res signifie planter longuement le décor avant toute action.
items.tip: In medias res means the opposite: dropping straight into action already underway.

items.prompt: Quel terme désigne les toutes dernières lignes d'une œuvre, qui répondent souvent à l'incipit ?
